title: Harvesting and storing garlic
subtitle: Lifting at the right moment, drying, and storing for months
excerpt: Garlic is harvested in June or July when the lower leaves have yellowed but the upper leaves are still green. Lifted too late, the cloves separate and the bulb stores poorly. After lifting, the bulbs need two to four weeks of curing in a warm airy place before long-term storage.
sourceNotes: RHS garlic growing guide (rhs.org.uk). Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), kitchen garden section. USDA cooperative extension notes on allium harvest and storage, public domain.

glossaryTerms.definition: Leaving freshly lifted garlic in a warm, dry, well-ventilated place for two to four weeks after harvest. Curing allows the outer skin to dry and papery, the neck to dry and contract, and the cloves to firm up. Properly cured garlic stores at room temperature for three to nine months depending on variety. Uncured garlic must be used within a few weeks.

content.text: The harvest window for garlic is about two weeks: lift too early and the cloves are small; lift too late and the bulb has divided fully, the cloves have started to separate, and storing quality drops sharply. The right moment is when about half the leaves have yellowed from the bottom up and the remaining upper leaves are still green.

Check plants from mid-June. Autumn-planted UK garlic is usually ready late June to mid-July. Count the leaves: a garlic plant has one leaf per clove. When four or five lower leaves have turned yellow and the remaining five or six are still green, lift a test bulb. If the wrapper skin is tight and papery and the bulb segments (cloves) are well defined through the skin, the rest are ready. Don't wait for all the leaves to die down.

Choose a dry day if possible. Loosen the soil with a fork a few centimetres away from the bulb before lifting; garlic skins bruise and tear easily against the tines. Hold by the top growth, not the bulb neck. Any cuts or damage to the bulb skin will cause the damaged bulb to rot in storage; use damaged bulbs fresh first.
Leave the bulbs on the soil surface in dry weather for two to three days, then move to a warm, dry, airy place for a further two to four weeks to
fully. A greenhouse bench, shed shelf, or airy porch works well. Lay them out in a single layer or hang in bunches. Don't dry in direct rain; cover if a wet week is forecast.

Once the skins are dry and papery and the necks are completely dry, trim the roots and cut or plait the tops. Store in a cool (10 to 15°C), dry, well-ventilated place: a larder, shed, or garage. Hardneck varieties store for three to five months; softneck varieties can store six to nine months if well cured. Check stored bulbs every two to three weeks and remove any that show soft spots.
